transcript: Your database has been doing a full table scan on every single request since you launched it. You didn't even notice until your hosting provider throttled you for excessive resource usage on their platform. So your AI wrote the queries, right? They worked, pages loaded, data showed up. What you did not see is that every query was reading every row in the table to find the one row it needed. So at 500 rows, that takes milliseconds, no biggie. At 100,000 rows, your server is doing the computational equivalent of reading every book in a library to find one title. So your hosting provider noticed before you did, started charging you for it. So your app is slow, your bill's climbing, and your users, they're leaving. Let's get it fixed. Step one, your AI never added indexes to your database. An index tells the database exactly where to find the data instead of scanning every single row. Without one, every query is a full table scan. The larger the table, the slower the request. So direct your AI to identify every query your application is running, and then determine which columns are used in filters and lookups and add those indexes to those columns. Test this before and after query speed, which is definitely going to increase. Test your actual data. Step two, your queries are pulling more data than your pages actually need. Your AI wrote queries that return every column on every matching row, even when the page only displays three fields. So every unnecessary column is data your server processes and your network transmits for no reason at all. What you need to do is direct your AI to audit every query and restrict the selected fields to only what the requesting page or features are actually using. That's a win. And step three, you have no visibility into which queries are slow. Your database has been running expensive queries since day one and you have no way to see them, right? Well, direct your AI to enable slow query logging, set a threshold, and build a dashboard that will show you which queries exceeded that threshold, how often they are running, and how much resource each one is consuming. Your database is working 10 times harder than it ever needed to. So let's make sure we index it before your hosting provider shuts you down.

claims.topic: Database query performance, resource usage, and observability in an AI-generated application
claims.problem: The speaker asserts that the application’s database access has been inefficient since launch: queries functionally returned data, but allegedly performed full table scans, over-fetched columns, and lacked slow-query visibility until hosting-provider throttling, rising costs, slow pages, and user loss exposed the issue.
technicalClaims: The speaker claims the AI-generated database layer did not add indexes on columns used for filters and lookups, causing queries to read every row in a table to find matching rows; this is described as harmless at about 500 rows but increasingly slow and resource-intensive at about 100,000 rows, with the larger table size directly increasing request cost and latency.

The speaker states that, without relevant indexes, each query becomes a full table scan, and that this scan-heavy workload is what made the hosting provider notice excessive resource usage before the application owner did, leading to throttling or higher charges.

The speaker claims the application’s queries return more data than pages need, such as selecting every column on matching rows when the UI only displays a few fields; every unnecessary column is said to create avoidable server-side processing and network transmission.

The speaker claims the system has no visibility into slow or expensive queries because slow query logging and reporting are absent, so costly queries have allegedly been running since day one without a way to see which queries exceed a threshold, how often they run, or how much resource they consume.
claims.recommendedSolution: Treating the speaker’s recommendation as a hypothesis to test: direct the AI or development process to enumerate every query the application runs, identify columns used in filters and lookups, add indexes on those columns, and benchmark query speed before and after using actual data; audit every query’s selected fields and restrict projections to only the fields actually used by the requesting page or feature; enable slow query logging, configure a threshold, and build a dashboard showing threshold-exceeding queries, their frequency, and their resource consumption.
reasoning: Functional correctness masked the performance issue: pages loaded and data appeared, but the speaker argues the database was doing unnecessary work because queries scanned entire tables rather than using targeted access paths.

The asserted mechanism for the indexing issue is that an index lets the database locate needed rows directly, while the absence of an index forces row-by-row scanning; as row count grows, scan work grows, so latency, compute usage, hosting charges, and throttling risk increase.

The recommended index audit is expected to change the access pattern from full table scans to indexed lookups for queries filtering or looking up rows by indexed columns; the speaker claims before-and-after tests on actual data should show query speed increasing.

The asserted mechanism for over-fetching is that selecting unused columns increases the amount of data the database/server must process and the network must transmit; restricting selected fields should reduce unnecessary processing and transfer for each request.

The asserted mechanism for slow-query logging is observability rather than direct optimization: by logging queries above a threshold and dashboarding frequency and resource use, the team can identify which expensive queries need attention instead of discovering the problem only through provider throttling or billing.
assumptions: The application uses a table/row/column-oriented SQL-style database where indexes, selected columns, and full table scans are meaningful concepts.
The problematic queries are discoverable from the repository or runtime configuration and can be mapped to the pages or features that issue them.
The queried filter and lookup columns are suitable for indexing, and the database optimizer would actually choose the added indexes for the relevant queries.

The performance and cost problem is materially caused by database query patterns rather than primarily by application code, caching, external services, hardware limits, or unrelated infrastructure issues.
The production-like dataset is large enough for scan costs to matter, and local or staging tests with actual data are representative enough to measure the claimed before-and-after effect.
The additional storage and write-time maintenance cost of new indexes is acceptable for this application’s workload.
The database or hosting environment supports slow query logging, configurable thresholds, and access to enough resource-consumption data to populate the proposed dashboard.
technologiesAndPatterns: SQL-style database tables, rows, and columns
Database indexes on filter and lookup columns
Query projection / selecting only required fields
Query performance benchmarking on actual data
Performance dashboard for slow queries, frequency, and resource consumption

implications.detail: If the speaker’s diagnosis is accurate, unindexed filters/lookups and full table scans increase request latency and database CPU/I/O, especially as table size grows.
If queries select unused columns, each request performs avoidable server processing and network transfer; narrowing selected fields should reduce that waste.
The workload may appear acceptable at small row counts, such as hundreds of rows, but degrade sharply as tables reach much larger sizes, such as 100,000 rows.

The speaker ties excessive database work to hosting-provider throttling, increased charges, and possible shutdown risk, making query efficiency an operational concern rather than only a code-quality issue.
Slow query logging and a dashboard would provide operational visibility into expensive queries, their frequency, and resource use, enabling targeted remediation instead of relying on provider alerts.

Because the speaker attributes the issue to AI-generated queries that worked functionally but lacked optimization, repository review should evaluate generated database access for performance characteristics, not only correctness.

uncertainties: Repository inspection can likely identify query definitions, selected columns, schema indexes, and whether slow-query logging is configured, but it cannot by itself prove that every production request performs a full table scan.
Whether specific queries actually use full table scans requires execution plans, database statistics, and production-like data, not only source-code review.

The speaker’s absolute claims that every query scans every row, that the database is working 10 times harder than needed, and that query speed will definitely increase are runtime-performance claims requiring measurement.

The causal link between the database behavior and hosting-provider throttling, billing increases, application slowness, or user departures would require provider logs, billing records, application telemetry, and user analytics.
The benefit of each proposed index depends on query shape, column selectivity, data distribution, existing indexes, database optimizer behavior, and the read/write mix.

The feasibility and detail level of the proposed slow-query dashboard depend on the specific database, hosting provider, logging permissions, and available resource metrics, none of which are specified in the transcript.

onboardingPrompt:
You are performing a read-only onboarding pass for a follow-up audit of database query performance, resource usage, and observability in this repository. Do not edit files, create migrations, refactor queries, tune indexes, or implement monitoring. Your task is to understand the current system and produce an evidence-backed architecture briefing. Do not assume there is a performance defect; map what exists and what cannot be known from source alone.

Scope your discovery to the parts of the repository that materially affect database access and operational visibility. First identify the application boundaries: runtime services, web/API entry points, background workers, scheduled jobs, serverless functions, queues, client/server split, deployment artifacts, and any local/staging/production configuration represented in the repo. Record exact file paths and symbols for frameworks, routes, handlers, controllers, service modules, repositories, ORM clients, raw SQL call sites, generated database clients, and data access abstractions. If this is not a SQL-style database application, say so and map the actual persistence model instead.

Build a concise data-access map. Identify the database technology and access pattern from evidence: ORM/query builder/raw SQL, schema definitions, migrations, model declarations, seed data, generated types, connection configuration, pooling, transaction helpers, multi-tenant or per-user scoping, and any caching layer that may affect query frequency. Inventory tables/models/entities that appear central to user-facing pages or high-volume flows. For each important entity, note defined columns, relationships, constraints, and currently declared indexes or unique keys, citing exact migration/schema files and names where available. Do not evaluate whether any index is sufficient yet; just report what exists.

Trace representative request/data/control flows from user entry point to database and back. Prioritize flows that render pages, load lists, search/filter records, look up records by IDs or slugs, authenticate users, hydrate dashboards, or run background aggregation. For each flow, cite the route/page/component/job symbol, the service or resolver it calls, the query-generating symbol or SQL fragment, the returned DTO/API shape if present, and the UI or downstream consumer that uses the data. Capture whether queries are assembled dynamically, hidden behind generated code, or issued through framework conventions that require further tracing.

Map query projection and serialization mechanisms without judging them. Identify whether the code typically selects explicit fields, whole model instances, relation includes, joins, eager/lazy loading, GraphQL resolvers, REST serializers, server components, or client-side filtering after fetching. Cite examples with paths and symbols. Note places where selected fields are not statically obvious because of ORM defaults, generated clients, spread operators, dynamic includes, generic repository methods, or external packages.

Map observability and operations relevant to database behavior. Look for application logging around database calls, ORM debug logging, slow-query or expensive-query configuration, APM/tracing integrations, metrics exporters, dashboards as code, log drains, provider-specific settings, alerting, sampling, and environment variables that control logging thresholds. Also note tests, fixtures, performance tests, seed volumes, benchmark scripts, EXPLAIN helpers, load-test scripts, and CI checks that could provide or approximate evidence about query behavior. Cite exact files and settings. If production settings are outside the repo, mark them unknown rather than inferring them.

Distinguish confirmed facts, inferences, and unknowns. Confirmed facts must include exact evidence such as file paths plus symbol names, migration names, route paths, model names, query method names, config keys, test names, or traced call chains. Inferences must explain why they follow from the evidence. Unknowns should call out missing runtime data such as table cardinalities, query plans, database statistics, production traffic mix, cache hit rates, provider throttling/billing data, and real slow-query logs.

Deliver the onboarding output in this structure:
1. System snapshot: technologies, services, runtime boundaries, database engine/access layer, deployment/config artifacts.
2. Data model and access layer map: key tables/models, relationships, indexes/constraints currently declared, query abstractions.
3. Request and job flow map: compact table of important flows from entry point to database query to response/UI consumer.
4. Query shape and projection patterns: how queries are constructed and how returned data is consumed, with examples.
5. Observability and testing map: logging/metrics/tracing/dashboard/test/benchmark evidence relevant to database behavior.
6. Evidence ledger: confirmed facts vs inferences vs unknowns.
7. Handoff map for the follow-up audit: the most relevant files, symbols, routes, queries, configs, and missing runtime artifacts to inspect next.

Be concise but specific. Do not propose fixes, do not rank severity, and do not test any recommendation in this pass. End with: STOP - waiting for the investigation prompt.
investigationPrompt:
You are now performing a read-only claim-specific investigation of database query performance, resource usage, and observability. Do not edit files, add migrations, change query projections, configure logging, write implementation code, run destructive commands, commit, or refactor. Use the onboarding findings as context, but independently verify every conclusion with repository evidence. Where proof requires runtime data, say exactly what runtime evidence is needed and do not fabricate results.

Hypothesis to test, preserving qualifications: the speaker recommends that the team enumerate every query the application runs; identify columns used in filters and lookups; add indexes on suitable columns; benchmark query speed before and after on actual data; audit each query's selected fields and restrict projections to fields actually used by the requesting page or feature; enable slow-query logging with a threshold; and build a dashboard showing threshold-exceeding queries, their frequency, and resource consumption. The claimed reasoning is that functional correctness can mask inefficient database access: unindexed filters/lookups may force row-by-row scans as table sizes grow; over-broad projections may increase server processing and network transfer; and absent slow-query visibility may delay discovery until provider throttling, bills, or user-facing latency reveal the issue. Treat all of this as a hypothesis, not as an established fact.

Applicability gate. First determine whether the repository uses a table/row/column SQL-style database where indexes, projections, and execution plans are meaningful. If it uses a different persistence model, mark SQL-specific claims Not Applicable and adapt only the observability/resource-use portions that still apply. Identify the database engine, ORM/query builder/raw SQL layer, schema/migration source of truth, and production configuration exposure. State what can be established statically and what cannot, including table row counts, data distributions, optimizer choices, production query frequency, cache behavior, and provider throttling/billing history.

Required status vocabulary for each material claim: Confirmed, Partially Applicable, Refuted, Not Applicable, or Needs Runtime Verification. Use Confirmed only when repository evidence is sufficient for the claim as stated. Use Needs Runtime Verification when static evidence suggests a risk or possibility but execution plans, metrics, logs, production-like data, or provider records are required. Include severity where meaningful: Critical, High, Medium, Low, or Informational, based on actual exposure, request frequency, table scale, exploitability or reliability impact, latency/cost risk, and operational cost. Do not exaggerate a theoretical full-table-scan possibility into a production incident without traffic, size, and plan evidence.

Investigate using the following claim-specific methodology.

1. Query inventory and flow mapping. Enumerate database query call sites as completely as practical: ORM model calls, query builder chains, raw SQL, stored procedure calls, generated resolvers, GraphQL resolvers, server actions, API routes, background jobs, scheduled tasks, authentication/session queries, and admin/reporting paths. For each query or query family, record: file path and symbol, entry route/job/feature, table/model(s), filters/lookups, joins/includes/relations, order/group/pagination clauses, selected fields if explicit, consumer UI/API fields if traceable, caching layer if any, and whether the query is static, dynamic, or generated. If the codebase is large, prioritize user-facing high-frequency flows and explain sampling limits.

2. Index and access-path applicability. For each query with WHERE, JOIN, lookup-by-ID/slug/email, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, foreign-key traversal, or uniqueness semantics, compare predicates and ordering to indexes/constraints declared in schema/migrations. Record exact index names, columns, column order, uniqueness, partial/filter predicates, included columns if supported, and migration/model paths. Distinguish single-column from composite index needs; note when an existing primary key or unique constraint already covers a lookup; note when an index may not help because of low selectivity, leading-wildcard LIKE, functions/casts on columns, broad range predicates, small tables, planner behavior, or cache/materialized data.

Static inspection can show that a query has or lacks an apparent matching declared index; it cannot prove that the database performs a full table scan. For any claim that a specific query scans every row, require EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE output, database statistics, representative row counts, parameter values, and production-like configuration. If these are absent, mark the access-path claim Needs Runtime Verification, while still recording static evidence such as no declared index on the filtered column. Assess the realistic impact by combining known or unknown table scale, query frequency, user-facing criticality, and write workload. Include index side effects: storage, write amplification, migration lock risk, build time, cardinality/selectivity uncertainty, redundant-index risk, and maintenance complexity.

3. Over-fetching and projection fit. Audit selected fields against actual downstream use. For each representative query, identify whether it selects all columns by ORM default, uses SELECT *, includes whole related records, returns entire entities to serializers, or explicitly narrows fields. Trace the returned object through API response, server-rendered page, component props, GraphQL selection, DTO mapping, or background computation. Record exact fields selected and exact fields consumed where statically knowable. Mark over-fetching Confirmed only where repository evidence shows unused selected columns are returned beyond the consumer's needs. Mark Partially Applicable or Needs Runtime Verification where dynamic serializers, generic components, client-side use, hidden ORM defaults, or generated code prevent full proof.

For impact, avoid assuming all unused columns are costly. Consider row count returned, column sizes/types such as large text/blob/json, relation fan-out, pagination, compression, same-process server rendering versus network API response, cache behavior, and request frequency. Runtime evidence needed may include payload sizes, database bytes read/sent, application serialization time, traces, profiling, and real traffic mix. Also assess side effects of narrowing projections: broken implicit consumers, lazy-loading N+1 behavior, authorization checks requiring fields, cache key/entity normalization assumptions, GraphQL resolver semantics, type changes, and maintenance overhead.

4. Slow-query and expensive-query visibility. Inspect repository evidence for database and application observability: database-level slow query logging settings, ORM query logging thresholds, APM spans, OpenTelemetry instrumentation, metrics exporters, log drains, provider/IaC settings, dashboards as code, alert rules, sampling, redaction, retention, and environment variables. Determine whether the system can answer: which queries exceed a threshold, how often they run, their latency distribution, rows scanned/returned if available, CPU/I/O/resource consumption if available, route/job attribution, and whether alerts or dashboards expose this to operators.

Do not treat absence from application code as proof of absence in production if provider-managed configuration lives outside the repository. If production logging/dashboarding may be configured externally, mark it Unknown or Needs Runtime Verification and list exact artifacts needed: provider console settings, database parameter groups, pg_stat_statements/performance_schema data, query logs, APM dashboards, log drains, billing/resource metrics, retention policies, and alert history. Evaluate operational constraints: log volume/cost, sensitive data in SQL parameters, sampling, threshold tuning, performance overhead, storage retention, dashboard maintenance, and on-call usefulness.

5. Causal chain and external-incident claims. Evaluate only what the repository can support about the chain from query shape to resource usage to hosting-provider throttling, increased charges, slow pages, or user loss. Static evidence may show query patterns, lack of visible observability configuration, or deployment resource limits. It cannot prove provider notice, billing increases, throttling, page latency, or churn. For those claims, require runtime and business evidence: provider notices, billing records, database CPU/I/O graphs, connection pool saturation, application latency traces, slow query logs, deployment throttling events, traffic volume, row counts over time, cache hit rates, and user analytics. If such evidence is not in the repo, explicitly mark the causal claims Needs Runtime Verification or Outside Repository Evidence.

6. Benchmarking feasibility. Identify whether the repository contains seed data, anonymized production snapshots, fixtures, load-test scripts, benchmark harnesses, query plan helpers, or performance CI. Assess whether before/after benchmarking on actual data is feasible without implementation. Since you must not change code, do not run migrations or create indexes. If safe read-only commands are allowed by the environment, you may inspect scripts and configuration; do not execute tests that mutate databases unless the environment is explicitly disposable and you state that no changes were made. Required runtime benchmark evidence would include representative dataset size, warmed/cold cache policy, query parameters, execution plans, latency percentiles, rows scanned/returned, CPU/I/O, concurrency, and comparison against current baseline.

7. Current mitigations, counterevidence, and alternatives. Identify mitigations already present: primary/unique keys, foreign-key indexes, composite indexes, pagination/limits, caching, denormalized read models, materialized views, full-text/search indexes, queueing, connection pooling, query batching, GraphQL selection sets, API DTOs, APM, provider-level logging, or database extensions. Identify counterevidence that weakens the speaker's diagnosis: small bounded tables, infrequent admin-only queries, indexes already matching critical filters, explicit projections already in hot paths, external observability likely configured, or performance risks dominated by non-database work. Consider safer or smaller alternatives where appropriate: targeted runtime measurement before adding indexes, enabling existing provider slow-query reports before building a custom dashboard, narrowing only high-volume/heavy-payload queries, removing redundant includes, adding pagination, using existing APM spans, or documenting production evidence gaps. Do not implement any alternative.

Report format. Provide a concise evidence-backed report with these sections:

A. Applicability summary: database type, data-access stack, whether SQL/index/projection/slow-query concepts apply, and key static versus runtime limits.

B. Material-claim matrix. Include one row per claim:
- Claim: missing indexes on filter/lookup columns causing scans that worsen with table size.
- Claim: scan-heavy workload caused provider throttling or higher charges before application owner visibility.
- Claim: queries return more data than pages/features need.
- Claim: slow/expensive query visibility is absent.
- Claim: the proposed audit, indexing, projection narrowing, benchmarking, and slow-query dashboard fit this application.
For each row include Status, Severity if meaningful, repository evidence with exact paths/symbols/settings, missing evidence, assumptions, realistic impact, counterevidence/mitigations, and confidence.

C. Query/index evidence table. For each prioritized query family, include entry point, query symbol, table/model, predicates/lookups/order, selected fields, existing relevant indexes/constraints, static concern or counterevidence, runtime evidence needed, and impact estimate.

D. Projection evidence table. For each prioritized response/page/job, include query symbol, selected fields or ORM default behavior, consumed fields, confirmed unused fields if any, dynamic unknowns, and impact factors such as row count, large columns, relation fan-out, or network boundary.

E. Observability evidence table. Include database logging/APM/metrics/dashboard/alerting artifacts found, thresholds if configured, attribution capability, resource metrics availability, gaps, and external artifacts required.

F. Static-versus-runtime boundary. Explicitly list conclusions established by source inspection and conclusions that require EXPLAIN plans, row counts, production-like data, traces, metrics, logs, profiling, load tests, provider records, billing, or traffic analytics.

G. Recommendation disposition: Proceed, Modify Recommendation, Reject, or Gather More Evidence. Justify the disposition. Prefer Modify Recommendation or Gather More Evidence when static evidence suggests possible issues but runtime proof is absent. Specify which parts, if any, should proceed only after measurement; which are already unnecessary due to existing mitigations; and which areas should remain untouched.

H. Open questions and requested artifacts for a follow-up runtime review. End with an explicit: STOP - read-only investigation complete.
